BOPEN.heard: Building virtual environments exam prep, key terms, the go-dough editor and scenes. 34 terms for building a game in go-dough from the panels of the editor to scenes, signals, the two clocks and collision. Knowing the exact term lets you tell an AI coding agent precisely what to change.

BIDEA.heard: Hollow, this is Lame in for Bear. Newcomers often say a scene is the running game. It is not. A scene is a saved tree of nodes, a file. What runs is the scene tree and it can hold far more. Godot is full of lookalike pairs like that one. This film goes through the terms group by group, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.

BDEFS.heard: Seven labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow. In the book text, the course text uses and explains the term. In the glossary, the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it. Editor or docs, the term comes from the editor itself or its official documentation. Computed, the numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs. Simulation, a model run step by step from stated rules, not a measurement of a real game. Illustrative data, numbers chosen to show the idea, not measured. Conceptual, a drawing of the idea with no data behind it.

B0101.heard: This table is the map, 34 terms about building a game in Godot in four groups. The first group is the editor with the scene doc, the inspector, the 2D, 3D in script views and the run buttons. It covers where you look and what each part is for.

B0102.heard: The second group is Scenes and Nodes, Project Scene, Nodes Script, Scene Tree, Instance, Group Auto Load, Resource, and Export Preset and Template. These terms say how a game is built and kept together.

B0103.heard: The third group is clocks, input, and signals. The process function and the physics process function, input action, just pressed versus held, polling, event driven, and signal. These terms say when code runs and how the parts of a game talk.

B0104.heard: The fourth group is bodies in contact. Area 2D, static body 2D, rigid body 2D, and character body 2D, then collision shape, layer, mask, bit mask, and area snapshot. These terms say what can touch what and what notices it.

B0201.heard: This is a drawing of the Godot editor. The scene doc, lit in red at the top left, shows the nodes of the open scene as a tree. Its remote tab switches that view to the game while it runs. Here the save scene has three nodes and the remote tab counts seven once mobs have spawned. For example, the Walker platformer's saved main scene looks almost empty and the remote tab shows the floor, the spikes and the player that code built.

B0202.heard: The file system dock lit at the lower left is your view of the project folder. Every file of the game is in it under the res prefix written res colon slash slash. The scene doc shows nodes and the file system doc shows files. For example, when an AI coding agent adds a new coin scene file to your game, it turns up in the file system doc and you can open it from there or drag it into a level.

B0203.heard: The inspector on the right is where you see and change the properties of whichever node is selected. Here the player is selected and its speed is edited from 160 to 192. That is one number changed in one place. For example, select a moving platform in your level and the inspector shows its position and its collision layer ready to change by hand.

B0204.heard: The Node Dock shares the right side with the Inspector on the tab named Node. It tells you which signals the selected node has where each is connected and which groups the node belongs to. Here the player's signal named hit is connected to main. The Inspector is for properties and the Node Dock is for signals and groups. For example, to check that a coin's body entered signal reaches your score script, select the coin and look in the Node Dock.

B0301.heard: The same editor drawing with the top row lit. The 2D, 3D and script views are tabs that change what the main screen in the middle shows. In the 2D and 3D views you arrange a scene by hand and in the script view you write code. For example you place a platform by dragging it in the 2D view. Then switch to the script view to see the lines and AI coding agent wrote for the player.

B0302.heard: Output and debugger are the panels along the bottom. Output is the running log of whatever the game prints. The debugger is where an error is reported with the file in line it came from. Here it reports an error on line 12 of the player script. For example, if your player script prints at speed when it starts, that text lands in output and if the script calls a node that does not exist, the error lands in the debugger.

B0303.heard: Project Settings holds values for the whole project, not for one node. The drawing opens it from the project menu and lists four of them. 60 physics ticks per second, a name for physics layer 4 and auto load and an input action. For example, the Walker game names its physics layer 4 hazard in project settings, so you and the agent can call the spikes layer by name.

B0304.heard: The Run and Play buttons sit at the top right. Run Project, also the F5 key, plays the whole game starting at its main scene. Run Current Scene plays just the scene open in front of you. In the drawing, the first button runs the game with its mobs, and the second runs the player scene alone. For example, to test a new enemy's patrol without playing the whole level, open the enemy scene and press Run Current Scene.

B0401.heard: This is a folder listing. A project in Go-Do is simply a folder. What makes it a project is a file named project.goddot at the top of it. The res prefix written res colon slash slash always means that folder. For example, in the Walker Jumpman repository, the project is the Godot subfolder, so every test run from the command line has to point at that subfolder.

B0402.heard: A scene is a tree of nodes saved to a file so it can be reused, such as a level, a character, or a menu. Godot saves it as text, and each line that begins with the word node becomes one node. Here three lines make three nodes main, player, and mob timer. For example, you save a coin as its own scene and place it many times in a level, and an AI coding agent can open that text file and edit it.

B0403.heard: A note is the smallest piece a Godo game is built from. Each note is one object with one job. A sprite 2D draws a picture. A collision shape 2D holds a shape and a timer counts down. A scene is a saved tree of notes like these. For example, a coin in your game could be built from a sprite node for the picture. A collision shape node for contact and another node that plays the pickup sound.

B0404.heard: A script is the code that gives a node its behavior. In this course scripts are written in GD script. The gray ball has no script and sits still. The red ball script moves it right at 160 pixels per second. So after two seconds it has traveled 320 pixels. For example, the Walker player node carries a script that checks the jump action on every physics tick and sets the velocity.

B0501.heard: A small tree of nodes with columns of numbers. The scene tree is the whole hierarchy of nodes that exists while the game is running. A scene is the saved file and the scene tree is what runs. Nodes process from top to bottom the black numbers. The ready function runs for every child before its parent the red numbers. For example a main script can use its player and its HUD, the onscreen display and its ready function because the children are ready first.

B0502.heard: An instance is a copy made from a saved scene and placed in the running game. The box on the left is the template, the mob scene file. A mob timer triggers a new instance every half second until there are four. Then in this example the template's radius is edited to 45 and all four instances change. For example, in a dodge game every creep on screen is an instance of the same mob scene, so an edit to that scene changes every creep.

B0503.heard: Now the red instance has its own radius of 30. That is an override, a change made on one instance. When the template is edited to 45, three of the four instances follow it, and the red one keeps its own value. The override wins for that instance only. For example, you can make a single creep in a level smaller than the rest without touching the mob scene.

B0601.heard: This is a row of physics ticks across two seconds. Polling means your code keeps checking, tick after tick, whether something has happened yet. Here Maine asks 120 times whether the player was hit and only the red tick says yes. For example, the Walker game use is polling for its spikes. On every physics tick a script asks whether the hazard is overlapping the player.

B0602.heard: Event-driven means your code waits and runs only when it is told that something happened. Nobody asks. On the lower line there is one call at TIC 72, the moment of the hit. Polling asked 120 times for the same news. For example, a pause menu that does nothing until a key press arrives is event-driven, and so is a coin whose pickup code runs only when a body enters it.

B0603.heard: A signal is a node's way of announcing by name that something happened to it. Other nodes connect to the signal and each connection says who listens. The diagram shows five connections into main from the player, the timers, and the HUD. No node reaches into another. For example, in a dodge game the player emits a signal named hit when a creep touches it, and that signal is connected to the game over function in main.

B0701.heard: These are timelines for slow machine and a fast one across a quarter of a second. Godo calls the process function each time it draws a frame so how often it runs depends on the machine. At 30 frames per second it is called 7 times. At 144 it is called 36 times. For example a coin spin or a fading menu can go in the process function because it only has to look smooth. The system is designed to make it easy to make it easy to make it easy to make it easy to make it easy to

B0702.heard: Godot calls the physics process function on a steady clock, 60 times a second unless you change it. The red marks show it. Both machines get 15 physics ticks in that quarter second, however many frames they draw. Collision, forces and movement that must repeat exactly belong here. For example, the Walker player runs and jumps inside the physics process function, so a jump plays out the same on every computer.

B0703.heard: Now the bars show distance covered in one second. If code adds four pixels on every frame, the slow machine covers 120 pixels in the fast 1576. Multiply speed by delta, the time since the last frame and both cover 240. For example, an enemy patrol written as a fixed step per frame would walk much faster on a fast laptop.

B0801.heard: Keys and buttons on the left all connect to a box named Jump. An input action is a name for something the player wants to do, such as Jump with keys or buttons bound to it. Code asks about the action never the key. In this example, the space key, the W key and a Gamepad button, Pat et al mean Jump. For example, the Walker game binds space to its Jump action, so a Gamepad button could be added without touching the player's script.

B0802.heard: Just pressed versus held is a choice of button tests. In this example, the button is down for 30 ticks. Held is true on all 30. Just pressed is true on only one the tick the press began. For example, test just pressed for a jump, so holding space gives a single jump and test held for running, so the player keeps moving for as long as the key is down.

B0901.heard: A ball drops onto a dark floor in this simulated run. The floor is a static body 2D. It stays where you put it, whatever hits it, and other bodies collide with it. The ball lands and the floor has moved zero pixels. For example, the ground and the walls of the walker level are static body 2D nodes. The player stands on them and runs into them, and they never shift.

B0902.heard: The red ball is a rigid body 2D. The physics engine is in charge of it. You give it a force or a starting velocity and the engine works out where it goes. Here gravity pulls the ball down and it bounces five times before it settles. For example, the creeps in a dodge game are rigid body 2D nodes. Each one is given a velocity when it spawns and the engine carries it across the screen.

B0903.heard: The red block is a character body 2D. It goes only where your code sends it. The code sets a velocity and then move and slide carries the body and keeps it sliding along whatever it hits. Here the block comes down meets the floor and runs along it to the wall. For example, the Walker player is a character body 2D, which is why it's run speed and it's jump or numbers in a script, not forces.

B0904.heard: The pink box is an area 2D. It notices when something overlaps it and can emit a signal, but it never stops or pushes anything. The ball passes straight through. The area reports body entered, then body exited, and the ball's speed never changes. Character body 2D blocks and an area 2D only reports. For example, the spikes in the gold flag and walker are area 2D nodes. Touching them is noticed and nothing stops the player.

B1001.heard: A player box faces a column of objects, each marked with a layer. A collision layer answers the question, where am I? It is the layer or layers an object sits in where others can find it. Yet it are numbers layers from one and code use is a value instead. So the spikes are on layer 4, which has the value 8. For example, the Walker game puts its spikes on layer 4, named Hazard, and its gold flag on layer 5.

B1002.heard: A collision mask is the set of layers an object looks at. It can detect another object only if that object sits in one of those layers. Here the player scans layers 1, 4, and 5 so it detects the floor, the spikes, and the goal. The coin on layer 3 in this example goes unnoticed. For example, if your player never notices a coin it runs through, check whether the player's collision mask includes the coin's layer.

B1003.heard: A bitmask packs many on and off switches into one number, with one bit for each layer. The value for layer n is 2 to the power of n minus 1, so the player's mask is 1 plus 8 plus 16 which is 25 and layer 4 is the value 8. The red row is the common mistake. For example, an agent that writes collision layer equals 4, meaning layer 4, has put the object on layer 3.

B1101.heard: A gray sprite has a red outline inside it. The red outline is the collision shape, the outline the physics engine tests for contact. The sprite is only the picture the player sees. In this made up example the art grows to 128 pixels wide and the shape stays at 54. For example when Walker's player art was swapped for a wide mascot, the collision shape stayed small so an arm can seem to touch a spike with no contact at all.

B1102.heard: An area snapshot means an area's list of overlaps is refreshed only once in each physics step, so it can be a tick-old. The top row is the truth, the player stops touching a tick-four. The middle row is the list, and on that tick it still says touching the red cell. For example, Walker once counted a second death right after a respawn because the list still held the spikes. The fix discards two ticks after a reset.

B1201.heard: Red and dark dots sit under a single line of code. A group is a label you can put on any number of nodes, so that one call acts on all of them. In this made-up example, the five red nodes are in a group named mobs. One call group line frees all five, and the three dark nodes are untouched. For example, when a dodge gamer starts, it clears every creep off the screen with that one call.

B1202.heard: An auto load is a script or scene that Go-Doh loads at the start and keeps when the game changes scene. Here a menu and then the levels run in turn. Each scene's own variable starts over while the auto load score keeps adding up to 12 in this example. For example, a global script that carries the score from level to level, or one that handles every change of scene, is an auto load.

B1203.heard: A resource is a bundle of data with a declared type that several nodes can share. You write your own by extending the resource class. Change the tuning resource's speed once to 192 and the player and the HUD both get it while the test keeps it typed in 160. Unlike an auto load, a resource's data, not a node. For example, Walker's tuning resource holds the run speed, and one of its tests carries its own copy of that number.

B1204.heard: An Export Preset is the save set of choices for building the game for one platform, which files to include where the output goes and the options. An Export Template is the ready-made engine for that platform without the editor that your project's data is packed into. Preset, template, and project combine into the exported game, for example to ship your platformer for the web you write a web preset. And the export still fails until the templates for your exact engine version are installed.

B1301.heard: Each pair sets look alike terms side by side. A scene is a saved tree of nodes in a file. The scene tree is the running tree while the game plays. In Walker, the saved main scene holds one node, and the running game holds at least 13.

B1302.heard: The process function runs once per frame and its rate varies. On the left, seven calls with uneven gaps. The physics process function runs at a fixed rate, 60 a second. On the right, 15 calls with equal gaps.

B1303.heard: A collision layer says where an object is. It labels the player as layer 2. A collision mask says what an object scans for. Here the player scans layers 1, 4, and 5. The layer is where I am, and the mask is what I notice.

B1304.heard: The collision shape is what physics uses. In this drawing, the red capsule stays 54 pixels wide. The sprite is what the player sees. The gray art scales up to 128 pixels wide, and the shape does not follow. New art never changes the contact by itself.

B1401.heard: A vague request sits above the exact instruction that replaces it beside a chart of what it does. Make the player touch the coin becomes, put the coin on layer 2 and add 2 to the player's collision mask so one becomes 3. Mask 1, no contact. Mask 3, yes.

B1402.heard: Make movement the same on every computer becomes. Move in the physics process function. 60 ticks a second on any machine. The process function ran seven times on one machine and 36 on the other. The physics process function ran 15 times on both.

B1403.heard: Jump when I press space becomes, bind space to the input action named jump and test just pressed on each tick. For press of half a second, held is true on 30 ticks, so 30 jumps, just pressed is true on one.

B1404.heard: Tell the main scene when the player dies becomes, the player emits a signal named hit, connect it to the game over function in main and do not poll. Over two seconds polling asks 120 questions. The signal makes one call.

B1405.heard: Show me what the game really contains becomes Run It, switch the Scene Dock to its Remote Tab and Count. The saved main Scene file holds one node. The running game holds 13 at least.

B1501.heard: This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you trust a change to a Godo game. First, check that the saved scene matches the running tree. Run the game and look at the remote tab of the scene doc.

B1502.heard: Second, check that movement which must repeat exactly runs in the physics process function on the fixed tick. In the process function it would differ from machine to machine.

B1503.heard: Third, check that the input is an action in the input map, not a raw key. Then decide whether you want just pressed true for one tick or held, true for as long as the button is down.

B1504.heard: Fourth, ask who emits and who connects. If code asks the same question on every tick, consider whether a signal should replace the polling.

B1505.heard: Fifth, check that the collision layer and mask use the bit mask value 2 to the power of n-1 and not the layer number. Then check that the collision shape still matches the art.

B1506.heard: 6. Thask whether the area's overlap list could be a tick-old and whether the shared number sits in one resource. Then say it exactly. Not make it collide, but layer 2, mask 3.

BVDT.heard: Let's recap, each editor doc has one job and the remote tab shows the running game. A scene is a saved file and the scene tree is what runs. A signal tells you once where polling asks on every tick. The physics process function runs at a fixed rate on every machine. A collision layer says where an object is and a mask says what it scans. The collision shape is what physics uses, not the sprite you see.

BHTF.heard: Quizmy on go-doh terms with short game-making cases one at a time. Use the terms scene, scene, tree, instance, signal, polling, input, action, just pressed, collision layer, collision mask, and collision shape. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me if I was right.

BOUT.heard: Key terms the Godot editor and scenes at Nick Bear Brown.
